## 22.1 Overview

Proportional symbol maps (also called graduated symbol maps) belong to a
family of thematic maps that use the visual variable of **size** to
represent magnitude differences for a discrete, abruptly changing
phenomenon — for example, counts of people or events. As with choropleth
maps, they can be drawn in two flavours: a **classed** version
(range-graded or graduated symbols) and an **unclassed** version (true
proportional symbols, where the symbol area is directly proportional to
the underlying attribute value).

In this hands-on exercise, we will build a proportional symbol map that
visualises the number of wins recorded at Singapore Pools' outlets using
the R package **tmap**.

## 22.2 Learning outcomes

By the end of this exercise, you will be able to:

- Import an aspatial data file into R.
- Convert it into a simple point feature data frame and assign an
  appropriate projection reference to the newly created object.
- Plot interactive proportional symbol maps.

## 22.3 Getting Started

Before we begin, make sure the **tmap** package and the other required R
packages are installed and loaded. We use `pacman::p_load()` so that any
missing packages are installed automatically.

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)
```

## 22.4 Geospatial Data Wrangling

### 22.4.1 The data

The dataset used for this exercise is **`SGPools_svy21.csv`**, supplied
in CSV format.

The file contains seven columns. The `XCOORD` and `YCOORD` columns hold
the *x*- and *y*-coordinates of Singapore Pools' outlets and branches,
expressed in the [Singapore SVY21 Projected Coordinate
System](https://www.sla.gov.sg/sirent/CoordinateSystems.aspx).

![](image1.jpg)

### 22.4.2 Data Import and Preparation

The code chunk below uses `read_csv()` from the **readr** package to
read `SGPools_svy21.csv` into R as a tibble named `sgpools`.

```{r}
sgpools <- read_csv("../Data/SGPools_svy21.csv")
```

After importing the file, it is good practice to inspect the contents to
confirm the import was successful. The chunk below uses `list()` for
this purpose.

```{r}
list(sgpools)
```

Notice that `sgpools` is a **tibble**, not a base R data frame.

### 22.4.3 Creating an `sf` data frame from an aspatial data frame

The chunk below converts the `sgpools` tibble into a simple feature data
frame using `st_as_sf()` from the **sf** package.

```{r}
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs = 3414)
```

::: callout-note
## Things to learn from the arguments above:

- The `coords` argument expects the **x-coordinate column first**,
  followed by the y-coordinate column.
- The `crs` argument requires the coordinate reference system in
  **EPSG** format. [EPSG: 3414](https://epsg.io/3414) is the Singapore
  SVY21 Projected Coordinate System. EPSG codes for other countries can
  be found at [epsg.io](https://epsg.io/).
:::

After conversion, a new `geometry` column is added to the data frame.

![](image2.jpg)

You can inspect the basic information of the newly created `sgpools_sf`
object using the chunk below.

```{r}
list(sgpools_sf)
```

The output confirms that `sgpools_sf` is a **POINT** feature class with
an EPSG ID of **3414**. The `bbox` line reports the spatial extent of
the data.

## 22.5 Drawing a Proportional Symbol Map

To produce an interactive proportional symbol map in R, we switch
**tmap** into its **view** mode.

The chunk below turns the interactive mode on.

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
```

### 22.5.1 It all started with an interactive point symbol map

The chunk below produces a simple interactive point symbol map — every
outlet appears as a red bubble of the same size.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)
```

### 22.5.2 Let's make it proportional

To turn the map into a proportional symbol map, we map a numeric
variable to the `size` aesthetic. In the chunk below, the variable
`Gp1Gp2 Winnings` is assigned to `size`.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)
```

### 22.5.3 Let's give it a different colour

The map can be enhanced further by using the `fill` aesthetic to encode
a categorical variable. In the chunk below, `OUTLET TYPE` is mapped to
the bubble fill colour, so outlets and branches are visually
distinguishable.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1)
```

### 22.5.4 Faceted maps with synchronised navigation

A neat — and somewhat lesser-known — feature of **tmap**'s view mode is
that it also supports faceted plots. The `sync` argument inside
`tm_facets()` produces multiple side-by-side maps whose zoom and pan are
linked.

```{r}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col = "black",
             lwd = 1) +
  tm_facets(by = "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)
```

Before ending the session, it is good practice to switch **tmap**'s
viewer back to **plot** mode.

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")
```
